The Large Family's nursery had never known such happiness. Nobody had imagined the pleasures that friendship with the little-girl-who-was-not-a-beggar could bring. Her adventures and suffering alone made her a treasure. Everyone begged to hear, again and again, the account of what had happened to her. From a seat beside a warm fire in a large, glowing room, listening to descriptions of an attic's cold could be quite delightful. Indeed, it must be confessed that they rather loved the attic. Its bareness and chill dwindled into insignificance whenever Melchisedec entered the tale, along with the sparrows and all that you could see by climbing onto the table and putting your head and shoulders through the skylight.

Naturally, their favourite was the tale of the banquet and the dream that turned out to be real. Sara first related it the day after she was found. Several children from the Large Family came to tea. As they sat or curled on the hearthrug, she told it in her own fashion, while the Indian gentleman watched and listened. When the story ended, she lifted her eyes to him and rested a hand on his knee.
"That's how it happened to me," she said. "Uncle Tom, will you tell us your part now?" He had asked her always to call him "Uncle Tom." "I haven't heard it yet, and it must be lovely."

So he described his lonely days, ill, bored, and irritable, and how Ram Dass had tried to divert him by telling him about the people passing outside. One child passed more often than anyone. She began to interest him, perhaps partly because another little girl occupied so much of his thoughts. Another reason was Ram Dass's account of following the monkey into the attic. He had spoken of its bleak appearance and of the child's manner, which suggested someone not accustomed to the class of life lived by drudges and servants. Little by little, Ram Dass discovered how miserable her existence was. He also learned how easy it was to cross the few yards of roofing to her skylight. Everything else had begun with that discovery.

One day he said, "Sahib, while the child is running an errand, I could cross the roof and light her fire. Imagine her returning cold and soaked and finding flames waiting for her. She would believe a magician had been at work."

The fanciful idea brought a smile to Mr. Carrisford's unhappy face. Ram Dass, delighted by that response, expanded his scheme, explaining how easily many other improvements could be made. His pleasure and inventiveness were almost a child's. Planning and preparing gave purpose and interest to days that otherwise would have dragged painfully by. On the night the banquet failed, every package stood ready in Ram Dass's attic. He kept watch with the person who was to assist him, his companion just as eager for this curious adventure. Ram Dass had been stretched along the slates, peering through the skylight, when the feast came to its disastrous end. He waited until he was certain Sara had fallen deeply into exhausted sleep. Then he entered with a dark lantern, while his helper stayed outside passing objects through. At the faintest movement from Sara, he shut the lantern's slide and lay flat on the floor. The children learned all this and many more exciting details by asking a thousand questions.
Sara said, "How glad I am. How GLAD I am that my secret friend was you!"

No two people ever became closer friends. Somehow they suited one another wonderfully. The Indian gentleman had never enjoyed anyone's company quite as much as Sara's. Within a month, just as Mr. Carmichael had predicted, he was a changed man. Life continually amused and interested him. Even the wealth he had thought an intolerable burden began giving him genuine pleasure. There were so many lovely things he could arrange for Sara. They shared a little joke about his being a magician, and devising surprises for her was one of his delights. Beautiful new flowers appeared in her room; curious small presents waited beneath pillows. One evening, while they were together, a heavy paw scratched at the door. Sara went to investigate and found a magnificent great dog—a Russian boarhound. Around his neck was a splendid collar of gold and silver, engraved with the words, "I am Boris; I serve the Princess Sara."

To the Indian gentleman, no memory was dearer than that of the little princess dressed in rags. Afternoons spent in happy gatherings with the Large Family, or with Ermengarde and Lottie, were wonderful. Yet the quiet hours when he and Sara read or talked together alone had a charm of their own, and many interesting things happened during them.
One evening Mr. Carrisford raised his eyes from his book. Sara had not moved for a while; she was sitting gazing steadily into the flames.
He asked, "What are you 'supposing' now, Sara?"
Colour bright in her cheeks, Sara lifted her head.
"I WAS supposing something," she replied. "I remembered that hungry day and a child I met."
A note of sadness entered the Indian gentleman's voice. "There were so many hungry days, though. Which one were you remembering?"
"I'd forgotten you hadn't heard," Sara said. "The day my dream came true—that one."

She then described the bakery, the fourpence she had found in the wet mud, and the little girl whose hunger was worse than hers. Her telling was simple and as brief as she could make it. Somehow, though, the Indian gentleman felt obliged to cover his eyes with one hand and stare down at the carpet.
When she had finished, she added, "I was supposing a sort of plan. There's something I'd like to do."
Mr. Carrisford spoke softly. "What is it, princess? Whatever it is you want to do, you may."

Sara hesitated a little. "I wondered—since you say I have so much money—whether I could visit the woman who sells the buns. Could I ask her, whenever hungry children sit on her steps or stare through her window, especially on those awful days, to invite them inside and give them something to eat? Then she could send me the bills. Would I be allowed to do that?"
"Tomorrow morning you shall arrange it," the Indian gentleman promised.
"Thank you," Sara replied. "You see, I've felt that hunger myself. And it's terribly hard when you can't even make it disappear by PRETENDING."
"Yes, my dear, yes," the Indian gentleman said. "It must be terribly hard. Try to put it behind you. Come down to the footstool by my knee, and remember only that you're a princess."

Smiling, Sara answered, "Yes, and I can give the populace bread and buns." She settled on the stool. The Indian gentleman—another name he sometimes liked her to use for him—drew her small dark head against his knee and gently stroked her hair.

The following morning Miss Minchin looked out and saw perhaps the very sights she most disliked. Her neighbour's carriage, drawn by tall horses, stopped outside his door. The Indian gentleman came down the steps with a small figure beside him, warmly wrapped in luxurious soft furs. Miss Minchin knew that little figure well; it brought back earlier days. Behind came someone equally familiar and particularly irritating to behold: Becky. As a delighted attendant, she now always escorted her young mistress to the carriage, carrying her belongings and wraps. Already Becky's face had grown round and pink.
A little later the carriage stopped at the bakery. Strangely enough, its passengers stepped out just as the bun-woman was again placing a tray of steaming-hot buns in the window.
The woman turned when Sara entered the shop. Leaving the tray of buns, she came behind the counter and looked at her intently for a moment. Then recognition lit up her kindly face.
"I do believe I've seen you before, miss," she said. "But then again—"
"You have," Sara answered. "You once let me have six buns for fourpence, and—"

"Five of them went to that beggar girl," the woman interrupted. "I haven't forgotten. At first I couldn't understand it." Turning towards the Indian gentleman, she continued, "Begging your pardon, sir, but few young people notice hunger in a face the way she did. I've thought about it often." To Sara she added, "Forgive me speaking so freely, miss, but you're looking rosier now, and—well—better than you did on that—that—"
"I am better, thank you," Sara assured her. "Much happier, too. And I've come because there's something I'd like you to do for me."
"Me, miss!" said the bun-woman, beaming. "Well, bless you! Of course, miss. What is it you want me to do?"
Leaning against the counter, Sara then explained her little scheme: the terrible weather, the hungry waifs, and the buns they could be given.
Watching her closely, the woman listened in open astonishment.

When she had heard everything, she repeated, "Well, bless me! I'd be delighted to do it. I'm a working woman and can't spare much myself, with so much suffering everywhere you look. But, if you'll pardon me, I've given away plenty of bread since that rainy afternoon just because I kept thinking of you. So cold and wet you were, and looking so hungry, yet handing out your hot buns as if you were a princess."
The words brought an involuntary smile to the Indian gentleman's face. Sara smiled slightly too, remembering her own thoughts as she had placed the buns on the ravenous child's ragged lap.
"She seemed so terribly hungry," she said. "Even more hungry than I was."
"Starving, she was," the woman replied. "Since then she's told me many times how she sat outside in the wet, feeling as though a wolf were tearing at her poor little insides."
Sara exclaimed, "Oh, you've met her again since that day? Can you tell me where she is?"

Her smile kinder than ever, the woman said, "Indeed I can, miss. She's right in the back room there, and she's been here a month. She's turning into a decent, willing girl. Given the life she's had, you'd hardly credit what a help she is, both in the shop and in my kitchen."

She went to the little back parlour's door and called. A moment later a girl followed her out and took her place behind the counter. It really was the beggar child, clean now, neatly dressed, looking as though she had not suffered hunger for a long time. She was shy, but her face was pleasant now that she was no longer a savage. That wildness had left her eyes. She recognized Sara instantly and stood gazing as though she could never take in enough of her.

The woman explained, "I said she could come here when she needed food. When she came, I'd find small jobs for her. She was willing, I discovered, and little by little I grew fond of her. In the end I gave her a place and a home. She helps me, behaves herself, and she's as grateful as any girl could be. Anne is her name. She hasn't another."
For several moments the girls simply faced one another. Then Sara drew a hand from her muff and offered it across the counter. Anne clasped it, and the two looked directly into each other's eyes.

"I'm so pleased," Sara said. "And an idea has just come to me. Maybe Mrs. Brown would let you hand out the bread and buns to the other children. You might like being the one to do it, since you know what being hungry feels like too."
The girl replied, "Yes, miss."

Somehow Sara felt that she understood Anne, though Anne said so little. She only stood motionless, gazing after Sara as she left the shop with the Indian gentleman, climbed into the carriage beside him, and drove away.
